iut_type: End Product (JUST.WILL device using a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32S3 third-party board), uncertified third-party board built on a certified SoC still requires RF PHY testing
customer_question: The module we're planning to use is the 'Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32S3' -- it already has Japan's radio-law construction-design certification, but I'm not sure about the Bluetooth side. Can you advise?
question_variants: Does a certified underlying chipset automatically make any board built around it exempt from RF PHY testing?
If the chip itself has a QDID, why would the board built around it still need testing?
actual_issue: The customer assumed that because their chosen third-party development board ('Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32S3') used a Bluetooth-SIG-qualified chipset internally, the board itself would also be exempt from RF/RF PHY testing -- but a search of the Bluetooth SIG product database found no registration for 'Seeed Studio' or the board itself, only for the underlying chipset.
plain_english_explanation: A search for 'Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32S3' and the manufacturer name 'Seeed' in the Bluetooth product database, and a SIG member directory search for 'Seeed,' both returned no hits -- indicating this specific board is itself an unregistered/unqualified module, even though the SoC it implements (ESP32-S3R8) is itself registered with its own QDID. Referencing that chipset's QDID does exempt the higher-layer protocol stack (LL, L2CAP, GAP, GATT, ATT, SM) from needing fresh testing, but it does NOT exempt the RF PHY layer -- because Bluetooth SIG qualification of a chipset only covers what was actually tested for that specific registration, and RF PHY behavior depends on the board-level implementation (antenna, RF front-end, layout) which can differ between an unregistered third-party board and the chipset vendor's own reference design. This meant the customer's chosen board still required a full RF PHY test (quoted at the full 51-item scope, ¥1,500,000, since the board's actual PHY mode support wasn't yet narrowed down) on top of the standard proxy registration and Compliance Folder fees.
consultant_answer: We searched for 'Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32S3' and the manufacturer name 'Seeed' in the Bluetooth product database and the SIG member directory, and found no registration for either -- this board itself appears to be unregistered/unqualified, even though the chipset it implements (ESP32-S3R8) does have its own QDID. Referencing that chipset's QDID exempts the protocol stack layers (LL, L2CAP, GAP, GATT, ATT, SM) from fresh testing, but not RF PHY -- RF PHY behavior depends on the board's own antenna/RF front-end implementation, which a chipset-level qualification doesn't cover for an unregistered third-party board. So your chosen board would still need a full RF PHY test, quoted at ¥1,500,000 for the full scope, on top of standard registration and Compliance Folder fees.
decision_logic: A Bluetooth-qualified chipset's QDID only exempts the specific layers actually covered by that registration (typically protocol stack layers); it does not automatically exempt RF PHY testing for an unregistered third-party board built around that chipset, since RF PHY performance is board-level (antenna, RF front-end) and can differ from the chipset vendor's own reference design -- always check the SIG product database and member directory for the actual board/module manufacturer's name, not just the underlying chipset, before concluding test exemption applies.
final_recommendation: When a customer references a third-party development board built on a known qualified chipset, search the SIG product database and member directory for the board manufacturer's own name (not just the chipset) before answering test-exemption questions, since chipset-level qualification does not extend RF PHY exemption to an unregistered board implementation.
risk_if_done_wrong: Assuming an unregistered third-party board is exempt from RF PHY testing simply because its underlying chipset has a QDID could result in an incomplete registration submission, since the board-level RF PHY behavior was never actually tested or qualified.
